procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order of the High Court of Judicature for the Province of East Punjab at Simla (Falshaw and Soni JJ.) dated the 23rd November, 1949, in Criminal Appeal No. 367 of 1949 upholding the conviction of the appellant on a charge of murder and confirming a sentence of death passed on him by the Sessions Judge of Ferozepore.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Judicature for the Province of East Punjab at Simla upheld the conviction of the appellant on a charge of murder and confirmed a sentence of death passed on him by the Sessions Judge of Ferozepore.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Pritam Singh appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's decision. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, stating that the case did not fulfill the conditions for granting special leave under Article 136 (1) of the Constitution.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court will grant special leave to appeal unless exceptional and special circumstances exist, substantial and grave injustice has been done, and the case presents features of sufficient gravity to warrant a review.

facts: The Supreme Court was asked to grant special leave to appeal a decision from a High Court in a criminal case.
law: Under Article 136(1) of the Constitution, the Supreme Court has wide discretionary power to grant special leave to appeal.
This power is to be exercised sparingly and only in exceptional cases to maintain a uniform standard across the variety of cases it hears (civil, criminal, etc.).

The Court established a three-part test for granting special leave: it will not be granted unless it is shown that (1) exceptional and special circumstances exist, (2) substantial and grave injustice has been done, and (3) the case presents features of sufficient gravity to warrant a review.
The Court noted that while it is not bound by the principles of the Privy Council, they can serve as useful guides for invoking this discretion.
application: The Court applied its three-part test to the specific appeal before it.

It found that the case did not fulfill any of the required conditions: there were no exceptional circumstances, no substantial and grave injustice had been done, and the case did not have features of sufficient gravity.
reasoning.conclusion: Because the case failed to meet the necessary criteria for granting special leave, the Supreme Court affirmed that it would not interfere with the High Court's decision and dismissed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether once an appeal has been admitted by special leave, the entire case is at large and the appellant is free to contest all the findings of fact and raise every point which could be raised in the High Court.

facts: The appellant's counsel, Mr. Sethi, argued the appeal on the assumption that once special leave to appeal had been granted, the entire case was open for review.
This assumption meant the appellant believed he was free to contest all findings of fact and raise any point that could have been raised in the lower courts (High Court or trial court).
law: The Court cited the precedent set by the Privy Council in *Ibrahim v. Rex*, which established that the grounds for granting leave to appeal and the grounds for the hearing of the appeal itself are on the "same footing."

The power of the Supreme Court to grant special leave to appeal under Article 136 is a wide discretionary power to be exercised sparingly and only in exceptional cases where substantial and grave injustice has been done.
application: The Court found the appellant's assumption to be "entirely unwarranted" and a "misconception."
Adopting the principle from *Ibrahim v. Rex*, the Court reasoned that it would be "illogical to adopt different standards at two different stages of the same case."

Therefore, the Court held that the points that can be argued at the final hearing of the appeal are limited to those that were considered fit to be urged at the preliminary stage when leave to appeal was requested.
The scope of the appeal is not automatically expanded to a full rehearing of the entire case simply because leave was granted.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that once an appeal has been admitted by special leave, the entire case is not at large. The appellant is not free to contest all findings of fact and raise every possible point. Instead, the arguments at the final hearing are restricted to the specific points that justified the granting of special leave in the first place.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, in an appeal by special leave, should act as a third court of fact and re-weigh evidence, especially when there are concurrent findings of fact by the trial court and the High Court.

facts: The case was an appeal by special leave to the Supreme Court.
The appellant's counsel argued that the Supreme Court should re-examine all the facts of the case.
The trial court and the High Court had already agreed on the factual conclusions (concurrent findings).
These conclusions were based on the credibility of witnesses who were seen and heard by the trial court.
law: The Supreme Court's power to grant special leave to appeal under Article 136 is a wide discretionary power to be exercised sparingly and only in exceptional cases.
Special leave is granted only when exceptional circumstances exist, substantial and grave injustice has been done, and the case presents features of sufficient gravity.
The Supreme Court is not an ordinary court of criminal appeal.
application: The Court stated that it will not, as a general rule, allow facts to be reopened, especially when two lower courts have reached the same conclusion on those facts.
The Court emphasized that it gives weight to the findings of the trial court, which had the advantage of seeing and hearing the witnesses to assess their credibility.

The Court explicitly held that it would be "opposed to all principle and precedents" for it to constitute itself into a "third Court of fact" and re-weigh the evidence to arrive at a different conclusion from the lower courts.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition that it should act as a third court of fact and re-weigh evidence. It held that its discretionary power under an appeal by special leave is not for re-evaluating factual findings, especially when there are concurrent findings by the trial court and the High Court, unless exceptional circumstances demonstrating a grave injustice exist.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court will grant special leave to appeal unless exceptional and special circumstances exist, substantial and grave injustice has been done, and the case presents features of sufficient gravity to warrant a review.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued that his case met these conditions by presenting elaborate arguments on the facts to show that the lower courts' conclusions were incorrect and that a grave injustice had occurred. He contended that the eye-witnesses were from a hostile faction, their statements were discrepant, and the appellant had been falsely implicated due to enmity.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, adopted by the court, was that the court should only grant special leave if these conditions are met, and that the present case did not fulfill any of them. The respondent pointed to the strength of the prosecution's case (credible story, 5 witnesses, prompt FIR) to show that no grave injustice had occurred.

arguments.issue_text: Whether once an appeal has been admitted by special leave, the entire case is at large and the appellant is free to contest all the findings of fact and raise every point which could be raised in the High Court.
appellant_arguments: The appellant proceeded on the assumption that once an appeal had been admitted by special leave, the entire case was at large and he was free to contest all findings of fact and raise every point which could be raised in the lower courts.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, adopted by the court, was that this view is wrong. Only those points can be argued at the final hearing which are fit to be urged at the preliminary stage when leave to appeal is requested, as it would be illogical to adopt different standards at two different stages of the same case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, in an appeal by special leave, should act as a third court of fact and re-weigh evidence, especially when there are concurrent findings of fact by the trial court and the High Court.
appellant_arguments: By presenting elaborate arguments on the facts (discrepancies in witness statements, factionalism, etc.) and asking the court to overturn the lower courts' conclusions, the appellant was implicitly asking the Supreme Court to re-weigh the evidence and act as a third court of fact.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, articulated by the court, was that the Supreme Court is not an ordinary court of criminal appeal and will not generally allow facts to be reopened, especially with concurrent findings from two courts. It would be against all principles and precedents for the court to constitute itself as a third court of fact.

cases.principle: Cited for its review of the principles laid down by the Privy Council for granting special leave in criminal cases, which the Supreme Court found useful as a guide, though not rigidly binding.

Cited to dispel the misconception that once an appeal is admitted by special leave, the entire case is at large. The principle is that only those points can be argued at the final hearing that were fit to be urged when seeking leave to appeal.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Supreme Court's discretionary power to grant special leave to appeal is to be exercised sparingly and only in exceptional cases where it is shown that special circumstances exist, substantial and grave injustice has been done, and the case presents features of sufficient gravity to warrant a review. Once an appeal has been admitted by special leave, the entire case is not at large; only those points that were fit to be urged at the preliminary stage for granting leave can be urged at the final hearing. The Court will not generally function as a court of appeal on facts, particularly when there are concurrent findings by the lower courts.
obiter: While the Supreme Court is not rigidly bound by the principles laid down by the Privy Council for granting special leave, some of those principles are useful as a guide.

The only uniform standard that can be laid down for granting special leave across the wide variety of cases, such as civil, criminal, or income-tax, is that special circumstances must be shown to exist.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court's discretionary power to grant special leave to appeal under Article 136 is to be exercised sparingly and only in exceptional cases. Once leave is granted, the scope of the appeal is not automatically at large; only those points fit to be urged at the preliminary stage can be argued at the final hearing. The Court will not constitute itself as a third court of fact to re-weigh evidence, especially where there are concurrent findings from the trial court and the High Court, as doing so would be opposed to all principles and precedents.
legal_tests_applied: Generally speaking, this Court will not grant special leave, unless it is shown that exceptional and special circumstances exist, that substantial and grave injustice has been done and that the case in question presents features of sufficient gravity to warrant a review of the decision appealed against.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's assumption that once an appeal is admitted the entire case is at large was deemed 'entirely unwarranted' and 'wrong'. The Court held that it would be 'illogical to adopt different standards at two different stages of the same case.'

The appellant's request for the Court to re-weigh evidence and overturn concurrent findings of fact was rejected because the Court 'is not an ordinary Court of criminal appeal and will not, generally speaking, allow facts to be reopened.'

The Court concluded that the appellant's case did not meet the necessary conditions for special leave, stating, 'the present case does not in our opinion fulfil any of these conditions, we cannot interfere with the decision of the High Court.'

The Court found it would be 'opposed to all principles and precedents if we were to constitute ourselves into a third Court of fact and, after re-weighing the evidence, come to a conclusion different from that arrived at by the trial Judge and the High Court.'
why_respondent_won: The Court affirmed the principle that special leave is reserved for exceptional cases, finding that the prosecution's case was strong, supported by five witnesses, and believed by two lower courts, thus no 'substantial and grave injustice has been done.'

The Court adopted the respondent's position on the scope of the appeal, holding that 'only those points can be urged at the final hearing of the appeal which are fit to be urged at the preliminary stage when leave to appeal is asked for.'

The Court agreed that it should not act as a third court of fact, giving weight to the fact that the lower courts' conclusions were 'dependent on the credibility of witnesses who have been believed by the trial Court which had the advantage of seeing them and hearing their evidence.'
policy_considerations: On a careful examination of article 136 along with the preceding article, it seems clear that the wide discretionary power with which this Court is invested , under it is to be exercised sparingly and in exceptional cases only, and as far as possible a more or less uniform standard should be adopted in granting special leave in the wide range of matters which can come up before it under this article.

The only uniform standard which in our opinion can be laid down in the circumstances is that Court should grant special leave to appeal only in those cases where special circumstances are shown to exist.
